questions.stem: An attacker records packet timings between two hosts but never changes any packet. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Observing traffic without altering resources is passive; traffic analysis is the classic case.

questions.stem: Which attack primarily threatens availability by destroying or blocking access to an asset?
questions.explanation: Interruption is the availability-oriented attack (DoS flavour).

questions.stem: In security terminology, confidentiality, authentication, and non-repudiation are examples of:
questions.explanation: Services are the abstract goals; mechanisms are the concrete techniques that achieve them.

questions.stem: Encryption used to keep message contents secret is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Encryption is a mechanism; the service it mainly supports is confidentiality.

questions.stem: Classical encryption techniques are built mainly from which two families of operations?
questions.explanation: Classical ciphers rearrange (transpose) and/or replace (substitute) symbols under a key.

questions.stem: Kerckhoffs’ modern design assumption treats which item as public knowledge?
questions.explanation: Assume the adversary knows the algorithm; secrecy lives in the key.

questions.stem: A cipher that uses one fixed substitution alphabet for the entire message is:
questions.explanation: Monoalphabetic = one mapping for all positions; polyalphabetic varies the alphabet.

questions.stem: Why is the Caesar cipher especially weak against brute force?
options: Its nontrivial key space is only 25 letter shifts
questions.explanation: Only 25 nontrivial shifts of the alphabet — exhaustive search is trivial.

questions.stem: A scheme that keeps the same letters but changes only their order is a:
questions.explanation: Transposition permutes positions; symbol identities stay the same.

questions.stem: In columnar transposition, a keyword is typically used to:
options: Order the columns when reading out ciphertext
questions.explanation: The keyword (or its alphabetical order) selects the column read order.

questions.stem: An adversary who already has several matching plaintext–ciphertext pairs is using which attack model?
questions.explanation: Known-plaintext assumes the attacker has pairs; ciphertext-only has none.

questions.stem: Trying every key until decryption yields readable text is called:
questions.explanation: Brute force enumerates the key space.

questions.stem: Steganography primarily aims to hide:
options: The existence of a secret message in cover media
questions.explanation: Stego hides presence; cryptography hides meaning.

questions.stem: Altering least-significant bits of image pixels to embed a secret is an example of:
questions.explanation: LSB embedding is a common image steganography method.

questions.stem: Encrypting a continuous bit stream by XOR with a running keystream describes a:
questions.explanation: Stream ciphers typically combine plaintext with a keystream (often XOR).

questions.stem: Reusing the same stream-cipher keystream for two different messages is dangerous because:
options: XOR of the two ciphertexts can leak plaintext relationship
questions.explanation: C1⊕C2 = P1⊕P2 when the same keystream is reused — catastrophic.

questions.stem: Recovering a key by measuring power consumption of a chip during AES is an example of:
questions.explanation: Side channels exploit physical leakage (power, timing, EM), not only the cipher maths.

questions.stem: A TPM or secure element is best described as:
options: Dedicated hardware that isolates keys and crypto operations
questions.explanation: Hardware roots of trust store keys and perform crypto in isolation.

questions.stem: A product cipher in Shannon’s sense typically combines:
questions.explanation: Product ciphers compose substitution (confusion) and permutation (diffusion).

questions.stem: The key schedule of a block cipher is responsible for:
options: Deriving round keys from the master key
Choosing the IV randomly each year
questions.explanation: Key schedule expands/derives per-round keys from the master key.

questions.stem: Shannon’s confusion primarily aims to:
options: Spread one plaintext bit across many ciphertext bits
Hide the relationship between key and ciphertext
Remove the need for an IV
questions.explanation: Confusion obscures key–ciphertext dependence (often via S-boxes).

questions.stem: Diffusion in a block cipher means:
options: Using a public key for encryption
Spreading the influence of plaintext bits widely in the ciphertext
questions.explanation: Diffusion spreads plaintext influence; confusion hides key linkage.

questions.stem: In a Feistel structure, decryption is performed by:
options: Running the same structure with round keys in reverse order
questions.explanation: Feistel decryption = same round structure, reverse key order.

questions.stem: A Feistel round typically splits the block into halves and:
options: Encrypts only the left half with RSA
Applies a round function to one half and XORs into the other, then swaps
Requires an odd number of bits only
questions.explanation: Classic Feistel: F(right, Ki) XORed into left, then swap.

questions.stem: DES encrypts data in blocks of:
questions.explanation: DES: 64-bit blocks, 56-bit effective key (64 with parity bits).

questions.stem: DES is structurally best described as:
questions.explanation: DES is the classic Feistel block cipher.

questions.stem: The main practical weakness that retired single-DES for bulk encryption is:
options: 56-bit key space is searchable by modern brute force
questions.explanation: 56-bit keys are within reach of exhaustive search.

questions.stem: Complementarity and weak/semi-weak keys are discussed mainly under:
options: Strength and structural properties of DES
questions.explanation: DES strength topics include key size, weak keys, and related structural issues.

questions.stem: Differential cryptanalysis studies how:
options: Input differences propagate to output differences through cipher rounds
questions.explanation: It tracks difference propagation to recover key material.

questions.stem: Differential cryptanalysis is primarily a concern for designers of:
options: Symmetric block ciphers and their S-boxes/rounds
questions.explanation: It targets iterative block-cipher structure (historically DES).

questions.stem: Which mode encrypts each plaintext block independently under the same key?
questions.explanation: ECB has no chaining — identical blocks → identical ciphertext.

questions.stem: CBC mode needs an IV mainly to:
options: Randomise the first block so identical messages don’t start the same
questions.explanation: IV (and chaining) hide patterns across messages/blocks.

questions.stem: Triple DES (3DES) typically applies DES:
options: Three times (EDE) with two or three keys to stretch effective strength
questions.explanation: EDE with 2 or 3 keys is the standard 3DES construction.

questions.stem: Compared with AES, 3DES is generally:
options: Faster and preferred for new designs
Slower and retained mainly for legacy interoperability
Immune to all attacks by definition
questions.explanation: 3DES is legacy; AES is the modern standard block cipher.

questions.stem: AES (Rijndael) is best classified as:
questions.explanation: AES is an SPN (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey).

questions.stem: Which AES step provides the main byte-level nonlinear confusion?
questions.explanation: SubBytes is the nonlinear S-box layer.

questions.stem: Fermat’s Little Theorem is useful in RSA-related number theory because it relates:
options: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p not dividing a
questions.explanation: Fermat: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p under the stated conditions.

questions.stem: Euler’s totient φ(n) counts:
options: Integers in 1..n-1 that are coprime to n
questions.explanation: φ(n) is central to RSA exponents.

questions.stem: The Chinese Remainder Theorem helps when you have:
options: A system of congruences with pairwise coprime moduli
questions.explanation: CRT combines residues modulo coprime moduli into a unique class mod product.

questions.stem: In RSA implementations, CRT is often used to:
options: Speed private-key operations using factors p and q
questions.explanation: CRT speeds decryption/signing with p,q.

questions.stem: A defining feature of public-key cryptography is:
options: One shared secret for both directions only
Separate public and private keys with hard inversion without the private key
questions.explanation: Asymmetric: public encrypt / verify; private decrypt / sign.

questions.stem: Public-key encryption is commonly used to:
options: Encrypt multi-gigabyte files directly for speed
Exchange or wrap symmetric session keys
questions.explanation: Hybrid crypto: public-key wraps a fast symmetric session key.

questions.stem: In RSA, the public key typically includes:
options: Modulus n and public exponent e
questions.explanation: Public key is (n,e); private includes d (and often p,q).

questions.stem: RSA encryption of message representative m is conceptually:
questions.explanation: Textbook RSA: c ≡ m^e (mod n).

questions.stem: RSA security fundamentally relies on the difficulty of:
options: Factoring the modulus n (or equivalent RSA problems)
questions.explanation: Factoring n (or related hard problems) underpins RSA.

questions.stem: Using RSA without proper padding on short/guessable messages is risky because:
options: Algebraic and guessing attacks become practical
questions.explanation: Padding (e.g. OAEP) is required for real RSA security.
